chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
title: March repertoire and first hearing ragtime, hokum and jazz records
summary: The Arkansas band played marches and patriotic songs; he knew Sweatman's records and ragtime turning into jazz, and his solid legit trumpet solos.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: North Carolina, yes. That was in 1917.
1917. But when you were back home in Arkansas and you were playing with the town band, what kind of music were you playing? Just the standard march repertoire?
March repertoire and standard numbers like Over There, Over There, the Yanks are coming -- da, da, da.
Yeah, all that stuff like that.
Had you heard jazz by this time?

Yes, I heard -- let's see, who did I hear? I heard the records -- Sweatman, I believe I heard him on clarinet. He was a great clarinetist I heard playing. At that time they called it ragtime. It was ragtime music. And then it went from ragtime to jazz, but some of them called it hoke. They called it hokum. Did you ever hear that name kicked around?

Hokum, yeah, they called it hokum, because I know when -- this white boy I know, he came to St. Louis and told me to teach him some hokum. And he's teach me some legit. Well, I didn't have to be taught legit because I played all this triple time solos, 'Honeysuckle Polka' and 'From the Shore of the Mighty Pacific' by Herbert Clark, and 'Old Folks at Home' in three variations, so I didn't need -- I
felt that I didn't need anything else, because, see I was pretty well up there on the trumpet.
